corpus.title: DR Congo: Trial of post-Ebola exposure drug underway
corpus.signal_text:
Democratic Republic Of Congo
At a medical centre in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s eastern Ituri Province, more than 250 people are taking part in the trial of a drug that could stop them from contracting Ebola.
They have all been exposed to the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus for which there is currently no licensed vaccine.
Experts see the trial as a critical step in the fight against what is the country’s deadliest outbreak of the disease.
“What motivated me to take part was the death of my uncle. When he died, the results were positive [for Ebola]. Since I was a contact case with him, this motivated me to come here,” said one trial participant.
Another said that she had seen families where, when a case is found, almost the entire house is contaminated.
“But compared to that, when I joined this EBO-PEP trial, I found that no one from the family found themselves sick with this disease. That is to say, these tests are working really positively in our bodies," she said.
The experimental antiviral pill being tested is a post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP, which is administered immediately after suspected contact with the virus. Investigating physician at EBO-PEP drug trial, Jacques Zawadi, said the overall feeling of participants was one of satisfaction.
"To identify a medication, to treat a disease that does not have medication, this gives hope. Most of the participants are happy to be with us and to be able to benefit from this treatment, although it is still a trial," he said.
The trial began in July and is one of several studies launched to try to fight the disease. Il aims to recruit nearly 1,000 adults or children over the age of 12 who have come in contact with a confirmed case within the last five days but have no symptoms.
Participants are monitored in-person every day for 21 days, with a final phone call or visit after 42 days.
At least 8,300 confirmed cases, including 4,000 deaths, have been recorded since this Ebola outbreak was declared in mid-May.
Congo started vaccinating health workers with the Ervebo vaccine which was effective during previous Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common virus.
Authorities have said Ervebo could offer some protection against Bundibugyo virus, but whether the vaccine can actually prevent the illness is still being studied.

En République démocratique du Congo, la riposte contre Ebola veut s'appuyer davantage sur les communautés religieuses, alors que l'épidémie approche le seuil critique des 4 000 décès pour quelque 8 000 cas confirmés. L’épidémie d’Ebola a franchi le seuil des 4 000 morts en République démocratique du Congo, pour plus de 8 300 cas confirmés. Le pays fait face à la plus grave flambée de son histoire. Malgré ce bilan particulièrement lourd, les autorités sanitaires congolaises se veulent rassurantes. corpus.title: Thousands flee Ebola-hit displacement camp in DR Congo – UN
corpus.signal_text:
Thousands flee Ebola-hit displacement camp in DR Congo – UN
Thousands of people have fled an Ebola-hit displacement camp in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), leaving it largely abandoned after clashes erupted during a security operation, the UN said on Thursday.
The Kigonze camp in Ituri Province had housed around 19,000 people. Residents began fleeing after security forces entered the site to search for weapons and suspected members of armed groups, with gunfire reported during the operation.
”The enormous challenge of halting the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo just became even harder,” the UN said.
An Ebola transit center at Kigonze was also destroyed by fire this week, further disrupting containment efforts. The facility, operated by International Medical Corps and supported by more than 50 staff, was used to isolate and assess suspected cases before patients were transferred for treatment.
Fighting has also hampered the Ebola response elsewhere in eastern DR Congo. More than 3,000 people have fled the Rhoe displacement camp in Ituri’s Djugu territory since clashes intensified on September 27, according to the UN humanitarian agency OCHA. At least four people were reportedly killed and seven injured.
The outbreak, declared a public health emergency in May, has spread to seven of the country’s 26 provinces, with Ituri remaining the epicenter.
As of September 29, Congolese authorities had recorded 8,224 confirmed cases and 3,982 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 48.4%.
On Thursday, the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) warned against interpreting a recent decline in reported cases as evidence that the outbreak is easing, saying insecurity has disrupted surveillance in affected areas. Of the 63 health zones affected, 45 were still reporting active transmission.
”Falling in this curve doesn't mean that the outbreak is totally under control,” Africa CDC’s Dr. Wessam Mankoula said. “We cannot say at this stage the outbreak is under control.”
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola and has surpassed the toll of DR Congo’s 2018-2020 epidemic. There is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the strain, although candidate vaccines and treatments are being studied, according to the World Health Organization.
